marble.name: Series vs parallel circuits
marble.subject: Science
marble.description: Describe and apply the rules for current, voltage, and resistance in series and parallel circuits, and explain the practical uses of each circuit type
marble.prompt: Can you explain why the lights in your home don't all switch off when you turn off one room's light, but a string of old-fashioned Christmas lights does go off if one bulb breaks?

cluster.summary: Your child is beginning to understand energy — observing how sunlight warms objects and surfaces, and designing simple structures to create shade and reduce warming effects.

misconceptions: Mixing up which quantity is shared vs added — e.g. thinking voltage is the same everywhere in series, or that current splits but voltage adds in parallel; the rules are crossed between the two configurations.
Believing current splits EQUALLY at a parallel junction regardless of the branches — it divides according to resistance, with more current through the lower-resistance branch.
Thinking adding a parallel branch reduces the total current — it INCREASES it (lower total resistance, more routes for charge).
Expecting parallel bulbs to be dimmer than a single bulb — each branch gets the full supply voltage, so each is as bright as a lone bulb (unlike series, where they share and dim).
The current-used-up error resurfacing in series — thinking the bulb nearest the battery is brighter; in series the current is the same everywhere and identical bulbs are equally bright.
representations: Side-by-side series vs parallel diagrams of the SAME components, with ammeters and voltmeters placed at multiple points and their readings shown.
A junction close-up where branch currents ADD where they meet (the KS3 phrase made visual).
Brightness comparison — two bulbs in series (both dimmer than one) vs two in parallel (each as bright as one), with the supply voltage shared vs full.
Household/parallel wiring schematic — appliances each across the full supply, independently switched, with the 'unscrew one, the rest stay on' consequence.
A total-resistance dial — adding series components pushes resistance up and current down; adding parallel branches pulls total resistance down and current up.
authoredAnswer: In series the two bulbs share the battery's voltage, so each is dimmer than a single bulb; and because it's one loop, unscrewing either one breaks the loop and BOTH go out. In parallel each bulb gets the full battery voltage across its own branch, so each is as bright as a single bulb and the branches are independent — unscrew one and the other stays lit. probe: With two identical bulbs in a parallel circuit, both lit, ask the child to predict what happens to the SECOND bulb when you unscrew the first, AND why. The 'all connected, so all go off' child predicts it goes dark; the independent-loops child predicts it stays lit. Then unscrew one to reveal.

wrongAnswers.wrong: The bulb nearer the battery is brighter because it gets the current first and uses some up.
wrongAnswers.revealedBy: Predicts unequal brightness in series, with the nearer bulb brighter.
wrongAnswers.fix: Current is the same everywhere in a series loop (ammeters agree); the bulbs are equally dim because they SHARE the voltage, not because current is consumed.

wrongAnswers.wrong: If you unscrew one parallel bulb, the other goes out too, because they share the battery.
wrongAnswers.revealedBy: Predicts both parallel bulbs die when one is removed.
wrongAnswers.fix: Each parallel branch is its own complete loop to the cell; breaking one leaves the other loop intact — trace both loops.

wrongAnswers.revealedBy: Predicts parallel bulbs are dimmer than a single bulb.
wrongAnswers.fix: Parallel branches each get the FULL supply voltage; it's the current that adds, not the voltage that splits — each bulb is at full brightness (ideal cell).
